title: Hosted API streaming: stream rehydration failure postmortem (2026-08-07)
summary: On 2026-08-07 at ~15:12 UTC we observed a sudden, sustained increase in hosted API streaming TTFB and partial session stalls for ~37 minutes. A subset of streaming sessions failed to successfully rehydrate KV cache after edge reconnects, which inflated per-request compute and caused head-of-line stalls in the streaming multiplexer. This manifested as p95/p99 TTFB spikes, client reconnect churn, and ~14% elevation in 5xx for streaming routes. User-facing responses were delayed (median streaming initial bytes +420ms) and some long-lived streams timed out. The incident is classified P0 due to customer impact and the hit to SLAs.
impact:
- Duration: ~37 minutes (15:12 - 15:49 UTC)
- Affected surface: streaming endpoints on hosted API in us-west-2 and eu-west-1 (traffic routed through edge nodes with reconnect churn)
- Customer-visible: increased time-to-first-byte and intermittent stream freezes; short-lived elevated 5xx (14% relative increase vs baseline)
- Estimated requests impacted: ~62k streaming connections experienced degraded performance; ~1.6k sessions hit stream timeout errors
- Business impact: several high-throughput customers reported user-visible slowdowns; internal SLAs for streaming p99 latency breached during window
detection: Signal: automated streaming TTFB alert (p99 > 1.0s) fired at 15:14 UTC. Oncall received PagerDuty alert and Slack #sre-streaming channel filled with early telemetry. Customers also filed support tickets starting 15:18 UTC. Initial dashboards showed a correlated spike in edge reconnect rate and KV cache miss rate for rehydrations.
timeline:
- 15:12 UTC: first anomalous rise seen in streaming TTFB metrics (automated detection threshold approaching)
- 15:14 UTC: p99 TTFB alert fires; oncall page triggered
- 15:15-15:20 UTC: engineers collect traces and flame graphs; identify elevated rehydration miss rate for reconnecting sessions
- 15:22 UTC: short-lived mitigation: increase rehydration RPC timeout and enable conservative fallback to uncached execution path for streams showing rehydration failures (manual config change)
- 15:28 UTC: partial reduction in head-of-line stalls but p99 TTFB still elevated; further mitigation: throttle concurrent rehydration attempts per-edge-host to 8
- 15:34 UTC: metrics show progressive decline in p99 TTFB and reconnect churn
- 15:49 UTC: system returns to baseline; monitoring confirms stability for 1 hour
- 16:55 UTC: post-incident analysis meeting begins (warroom)
- 2026-08-10: final report published
root_cause:
A sequence of contributing factors led to production-visible degradation: 
1) A recent change to the edge streaming reconnect path (deployed 2026-07-29) added parallelized rehydration attempts for speed, but under reconnect storms this allowed many simultaneous cache rehydration RPCs to the KV service from the same edge host.
2) The KV service had an under-provisioned connection limit per-front-end and an internal throttling heuristic that began rejecting/queuing rehydration requests under burst. The edge clients did not back off quickly, causing long RPC latencies.
3) The streaming multiplexer holds serialized write/flush ordering for a connection; when one rehydration RPC blocks, it effectively stalls other streams multiplexed over the same worker thread, causing head-of-line blocking and elevated TTFB.
4) Monitoring thresholds for rehydration miss rate were present but not routed to an automated circuit breaker; there was no automatic fallback to a safe slower path when RPC latencies exceeded the rehydration timeout.
immediate_actions:
- Increased rehydration RPC timeout to avoid tight failure loops (15:22 UTC)
- Enabled uncached fallback route for streams that failed rehydration to avoid infinite stalls (15:22-15:25 UTC)
- Rate-limited concurrent rehydration attempts per edge host to 8 (15:28 UTC)
- Rotated a small pool of KV frontends to shift traffic while capacity adjustments completed (15:30 UTC)
- Notified customer success and engineering stakeholders and opened JIRA ticket for follow-up (JIRA-INC-4312)
short_term_remediation:
- Increase per-KV-front connection caps during burst windows (config change scheduled)
- Add a conservative exponential backoff in edge rehydration logic to reduce thundering herd behavior
- Add an automated circuit to detect sustained rehydration RPC latency and force fallback to uncached execution to protect multiplexers
- Expand runbook checklist for streaming reconnect storms (quick steps for rate-limiting rehydration and rotating KV frontends)
long_term_actions:
- Rework rehydration architecture: move from synchronous per-stream rehydration to probabilistic prewarming and shared prefix cache to reduce N x M RPCs during reconnect storms (RFC due 2026-09-01)
- Implement per-edge adaptive concurrency controller that reacts to KV backend latencies
- Improve throttling and autoscale behavior on KV frontends to better absorb reconnect bursts
- Add synthetic chaos tests that simulate mass reconnects + KV backend latency to validate protections before deploy
monitoring_and_alerting_changes:
- New alert: rehydration RPC latency p95 > 250ms AND rehydration miss rate > 5% in a 3m window -> page eng-sre and trigger automated fallback
- Dashboard panels for rehydration concurrency by edge-host and per-region KV rejection rate
- Instrument streaming multiplexer stall metrics (blocked-time percent) and add p95/p99 to SLO smoke checks
runbook_updates:
- Added section: "Reconnect storm triage" with ordered steps: 1) confirm rehydration miss-rate and source edge hosts; 2) apply per-edge rehydration concurrency limit; 3) enable uncached fallback; 4) rotate KV frontends; 5) notify CS customers and execs if >10% baseline impact.
- Included quick CLI commands and exact feature flags to flip for immediate mitigation
- Provided playbook snippets for increasing KV frontend capacity on cloud provider (permission notes included)
notes_and_questions:
- Why did the KV backend throttling heuristic not emit a high-priority alert? (investigate alert coverage)
- Consider whether deployment 2026-07-29 should have had a targeted canary that simulates reconnect jitter
- Customer outreach: coordinate with Customer Success for impacted customers; prepare clear explanation about fallbacks and timeline
- Runbook dry-run: schedule tabletop in next SRE rotation to validate steps
